analysis.one_liner: Requires a five-business-day wait and police background check before handgun sales, then a national instant check system.
analysis.headline: After two failed attempts to cut off debate, the Senate passed the Brady bill 63-36 through its House companion on November 20, 1993, and it became law.
analysis.plain_summary: The Brady bill would require anyone buying a handgun from a licensed dealer to wait five business days while local police check whether the buyer is legally barred from having a gun. People under a documented threat could skip the wait. Once a national instant background check system was built, dealers would check every firearm buyer against it instead. The bill also sent federal grants to states to computerize their criminal records so the checks could work.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities affected by gun violence gain a mandatory check of a buyer's criminal and mental-health record before a handgun sale, with an exception for people who can show they face a threat to their life or their family's. Lawful buyers gain a clear, uniform federal rule, and once the instant system is running, most purchases would be cleared quickly. Police chiefs get federal grant money to build the record systems the checks depend on.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: For roughly four years, licensed dealers cannot hand over a handgun until five business days pass while the local chief law enforcement officer checks whether the buyer has a criminal record or other legal bar to possession.

Buyers who present a statement from police that they or a family member face a threat can complete the sale without the wait, and buyers in states that already run their own verification system are exempt.

The Attorney General must build a national instant criminal background check system; after it is certified, dealers check every firearm buyer against it, with a three-business-day default if the system does not flag them.

The bill authorizes $100 million a year in grants to help states computerize criminal history records, and lets the Attorney General cut a state's crime-grant money by up to 50 percent if it misses its records timetable.
Records on lawful buyers must be destroyed within 20 business days, and no government agency may use the system to create a firearms registry.

analysis.who_pays: Licensed gun dealers bear new compliance steps: verifying identity, notifying local police, waiting out the five business days, and keeping records, with fines up to $1,000 or a year in jail for violations. Buyers without a qualifying permit wait several business days for their handgun. Dealers who do not deal in destructive devices pay higher license application fees. Federal taxpayers fund the grants and the national system.

drawbacks.text: Even buyers with clean records wait five business days during the interim period, a real delay for lawful purchasers that the bill's opponents in Congress pointed to; the threat exception covers only documented dangers.

Local police chiefs must make a reasonable effort to complete each check within five business days using whatever records exist, a new workload on local departments, though the bill funds state record improvements.
The bill raises license application fees for most firearms dealers and imposes penalties of up to a $1,000 fine or one year in prison on dealers who violate its procedures.
Until states computerize their records, checks are only as good as the paper records available, so the interim five-day wait offers weaker protection than the eventual instant system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is favorable to the public: a delay of a few business days and some dealer paperwork in exchange for a check that can stop sales to felons, fugitives, and people with disqualifying mental-health commitments. The bill guards against its own downsides by exempting people under documented threat, destroying records on lawful buyers, and forbidding a registration system. The main honest criticism is that the interim wait is a blunt delay that burdens all buyers, and its value depends on state records that the grants only gradually improve.

outcome.mechanism: Backers could not cut off debate on this Senate bill twice, so they passed the near-identical House Brady bill instead, 63-36, and that version was signed into law; this bill itself was indefinitely postponed.

narrative.text: Senator Metzenbaum introduced the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act on February 24, 1993, with 31 cosponsors including 4 Republicans.

On November 19, 1993, two cloture votes on the substitute amendment failed at 57-42 and 57-41, short of the 60 votes needed to end debate, with most Senate Republicans voting to keep the bill off the floor.

The Senate then agreed to the committee substitute by voice vote, incorporated the measure into H.R. 1025 as an amendment, and passed the companion House Brady bill, H.R. 1025, in lieu of this bill by 63-36.
The Senate indefinitely postponed S. 414 itself by unanimous consent, leaving the enacted version to be the House companion.
The companion Brady bill was signed into law later that month, creating the five-day interim waiting period and the national instant background check system.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people gained a federal background check on handgun sales: a five-day police check during the transition and an instant-check system after. Licensed dealers gained a uniform federal rule that applied to every sale. The effort to block the bill in the Senate failed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Buyers and communities gained background checks

for.name: Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act and managed it on the Senate floor.

for.name: Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage of the Brady bill (H.R. 1025), 47 of 56, after 48 of 56 voted to end debate.

for.name: Cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Republicans Kassebaum, Chafee, Hatfield, and Warner.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Championed the Brady bill and signed it into law in November 1993.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against cloture twice, keeping debate alive on the substitute amendment (57-42 and 57-41, short of the 60 needed); 28 of 44 still voted no on final passage.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Ran a major campaign against the waiting period, pressing senators to sustain the filibuster; the compromise version passed anyway.

against.name: Seven Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Joined Republicans in voting against cloture on both attempts.

sides.party_line_note: Democrats backed the bill almost uniformly (48 of 56 for cloture, 47 of 56 on final passage) while most Republicans opposed it (only 9 of 44 for cloture, 16 of 44 on final passage), though a Republican minority crossed over both times.

industries.industry: Licensed gun dealers and the firearms retail trade
industries.note: Dealers must verify identity, notify local police, wait five business days before a handgun transfer, and keep records, with fines up to $1,000 or a year in jail and higher license fees. Their trade association fought the bill because the checks delay and can block sales, which runs against the public-safety purpose the checks serve.

Sales to buyers the police flag are blocked and some sales are delayed by the waiting period, cutting demand at the margin, while lawful sales continue through the licensed channel. Manufacturers' allies in the gun lobby opposed the bill.

Police chiefs take on the interim background-check duty and must report multiple-sales records, but the bill authorizes $100 million a year in grants to computerize state criminal history records, money the check system depends on.
